There's a moment in translation work that fascinates me: when a word simply refuses to cross over. The Portuguese *saudade*, the German *Sehnsucht*, the Japanese *mono no aware*—these get cited so often they've become clichés, but the underlying phenomenon stays strange. A community of speakers carved out a piece of experience, gave it a name, and now people who grow up with that word may actually notice that feeling more readily. The vocabulary shapes the attention.

What I find most interesting isn't the untranslatable words themselves but what they suggest about all the experiences that *no* language has named yet. There must be thousands of them—feelings as distinct as nostalgia or schadenfreude, drifting through human lives unlabeled, noticed only as vague weather. The specific melancholy of finishing a book you loved. The small dissonance of hearing your own voice recorded. The warmth of seeing a stranger laugh at something you also found funny, across a room, without acknowledgment.

Some writers have tried to fill these gaps. John Koenig's *Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows* invents words like *sonder*—the realization that every passerby has an inner life as vivid as your own. Whether invented words can ever take root the way organic ones do is an open question. Language usually resists deliberate engineering.

But maybe naming isn't the point. Maybe it's enough to notice the unnamed things at all—to catch them briefly, hold them up to the light, and let them slip back into the wordless current of experience.
